wellby_spine.label: £16,300 at 2024 prices (HM Treasury's £13,000 at 2019 prices, uprated)
wellby_spine.provenance_note: GBP 13,000 per WELLBY at 2019 prices, HM Treasury Wellbeing Guidance for Appraisal 2021, page 33, taken directly. Applied at 2024 prices by the guidance's own footnote-102 method. The `value` field is documentation, not an input: no formula in the tool reads it. The WELLBY bands in `data.outcomes` were multiplied through at build time, so editing this number changes nothing on the page until those bands are rebuilt. check_drift.py asserts that the label still quotes it, so an edit here cannot silently leave the two disagreeing.

scenarios.label: Baseline (current system)
scenarios.desc: The current UK tax-benefit system, with no reform. Every other scenario is measured against this.

scenarios.label: Unemployment +3pp shock
scenarios.desc: Unemployment rises by 3 percentage points: that share of employed people lose their earnings.
scenarios.winlose: Losers are the households pushed out of work; a small share gain where means-tested support more than offsets a modest earnings loss.

scenarios.label: Unemployment +5pp shock
scenarios.winlose: Losers are the newly-unemployed households; a few gain where benefits more than offset the earnings lost.

scenarios.label: GDP −1% downturn
scenarios.desc: A mild downturn: market incomes fall 1% across the board.
scenarios.winlose: Losers are earning households; broad but shallow at this size.

scenarios.label: GDP −3% downturn
scenarios.winlose: Losers are earning households across the range; benefits cushion the lowest incomes.

scenarios.label: GDP −5% downturn
scenarios.desc: A deeper downturn: market incomes fall 5%.
scenarios.winlose: Losers are earning households; the loss deepens with the downturn.

scenarios.label: UC taper cut to 45%
scenarios.desc: Cut the Universal Credit taper from 55% to 45%, so UC is withdrawn more slowly as earnings rise.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are working UC households, who keep more of each extra pound earned.

scenarios.label: UC taper rise to 65%
scenarios.desc: Raise the UC taper to 65%, so UC is withdrawn faster as earnings rise.
scenarios.winlose: Losers are working UC households, who keep less of each extra pound earned.

scenarios.label: UC work allowance +20%
scenarios.desc: Raise the UC work allowance by 20%, so more earnings are kept before UC starts to taper away.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are working UC households with earnings around the allowance.

scenarios.label: UC standard allowance +10%
scenarios.desc: Raise the UC standard allowance by 10%: a higher basic UC payment for every recipient.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are UC households, concentrated lower in the income range.

scenarios.label: UC standard allowance −10%
scenarios.desc: Cut the UC standard allowance by 10%: a lower basic UC payment.
scenarios.winlose: Losers are UC households, concentrated among lower incomes.

scenarios.label: Raise income tax personal allowance
scenarios.desc: Raise the income-tax personal allowance, so more income is untaxed (a tax cut, shown as a gain).
scenarios.winlose: Winners are income-tax payers; the gain is largest for middle and upper-middle incomes and nil below the tax threshold.

scenarios.label: Remove High Income Child Benefit Charge
scenarios.desc: Remove the High Income Child Benefit Charge, so higher-income families keep their full Child Benefit.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are higher-income families with children whose Child Benefit is currently clawed back.

scenarios.label: Child Benefit +10%
scenarios.desc: Raise Child Benefit by 10% for every recipient family.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are families with children, spread across the range (Child Benefit is near-universal).

scenarios.label: GDP −3% with UC uplift response
scenarios.desc: A combined scenario: a 3% downturn together with a UC uplift as the policy response (a shock plus targeted support). One side of the headline crossover.
scenarios.winlose: Earning households lose from the downturn; lower-income UC households are cushioned or gain from the uplift.

scenarios.label: GDP −3% with tax-cut response
scenarios.desc: A combined scenario: a 3% downturn together with an income-tax cut as the policy response (a shock plus broad tax relief). The other side of the headline crossover.
scenarios.winlose: Earning households lose from the downturn; middle and upper incomes are partly offset by the tax cut, the lowest incomes gain least.

scenario_extra.html: At ε = 1.62, ‘GDP −3% with UC uplift response’ overtakes ‘Raise income tax personal allowance’ as the highest-welfare scenario (their welfare-effect ranking crosses there).

ui.single_note: Single-reform explorer. Exactly one control is active at a time: moving any slider, or switching the toggle on, resets the others to baseline. Combinations are not supported: the response surface is built from single-reform grids, which cannot represent how two reforms interact, so the tool will not let you set two at once.
ui.epsnote: ε = inequality aversion. 0 = every £ counts equally; 1 = a £ to a household at or below the poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much; 2 = about 2.8 times. Those are the maxima: living standards are floored at 60% of the median before the weight is taken. ε is a value judgement you set; the welfare number updates live as you move it. See the Home tab for detail.
ui.welfare_measure: What this measures: the pound value of the reform's effect on household welfare, where a pound of gain to a poorer household counts for more than the same pound to a richer one (ε sets how much more). It is distributionally weighted pounds, not simply the total pounds gained.
ui.scenarios_epsnote: ε = inequality aversion. 0 = every £ counts equally; 1 = a £ to a household at or below the poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much; 2 = about 2.8 times. Those are the maxima: living standards are floored at 60% of the median before the weight is taken. The scenario ranking reorders as ε rises (crossover at ε = 1.62). See the Home tab for detail.

capacity_caveat: The capacity and shock model is INDICATIVE. Its demand elasticities and staff ratios are registry assumptions rather than measured national figures, and the registry states no unit for the staff ratios. The shock anchors are this tool's own: both the modelled magnitudes and the share of {{UNITS}} losing an earner are computed from this country's shock run, and it is that share the three EU tools carry across in place of one of their own, applied there to each country's working-age unit count rather than to all its households, so that the base matches the one this share is measured on. Treat the demand, utilisation and gap figures as order-of-magnitude, not a local forecast.
provenance: Every figure traces to the canonical FRS 2023-24 microsimulation aggregates (PolicyEngine-UK; working-age benefit units, UC take-up calibrated to 0.731). Aggregates only; no microdata.
home_html:
About the project

BENEFITS develops a Holistic Appraisal Framework (HAF) to measure the social, economic and environmental value-added of social services. HAF combines real household microdata and tax-benefit microsimulation with “beyond GDP” valuation methods to quantify how policy reforms and social services affect people's welfare. Findings are consolidated through a Social Services Policy Observatory and citizen assemblies, supported by a Visualisations Platform, and built into a Policy Evaluation Toolkit to inform policymaking.

Full title: Building Economic, Needs-Based and Environmental evaluation Frameworks for Inclusive Transformation of Social services in Europe. Coordinator: KMOP, with 10 partners across 7 countries. Funding: Horizon Europe, grant agreement no. 101179032.

About this tool

This is the United Kingdom edition of the Microsimulation Valuation Tool. It lets you move each reform family continuously across its modelled range and read the distributional welfare, fiscal, and provider responses for the United Kingdom. It reads a pre-computed response surface ({{POINTS_PER_DIAL}}, each already passed through the welfare layer, computed on PolicyEngine UK over the Family Resources Survey 2023-24) and interpolates linearly between those points as you drag a slider. It does not run the tax-benefit engine live using microdata, and ships only aggregate welfare, distributional and fiscal results, no microdata. All monetary values are in 2023-24 prices, the survey year; no deflator is applied.

The {{DIAL_COUNT}} dials and the toggle

  • Minimum income: increases the Universal Credit standard allowance by 0 to +50%.
  • Child or family element: increases the Child Benefit rate by 0 to +50%.
  • Personal allowance: changes the income tax threshold, £12,570 in 2023-24, by −20% to +20%. A higher allowance means less income tax is paid, which the tool shows as a welfare gain; a lower allowance means more tax. The shipped “raise to £15,000” reform sits at about +19.3%.
  • GDP shock: reduces market income by 0 to 10%, routed through the GDP to unemployment transmission.
  • Unemployment shock: raises unemployment by 0 to 10 percentage points (pp).
  • UC taper rate: changes the taper across 45% to 65%, with the 55% baseline as the zero point.
  • UC work allowance: increases the work allowance by 0 to +50%.
  • Remove the High Income Child Benefit Charge: a binary toggle, off or on, not a slider.

One reform at a time

The tool enforces single-reform exploration: exactly one control is active at any moment, and moving any control resets the others to baseline. The response surface is calculated one reform at a time; combining two reforms is not the sum of their separate effects, because reforms interact, so the tool will not show a number it cannot stand behind.

Inequality aversion (ε)

ε sets how much more a £1 welfare gain to a lower-income household counts than the same £1 to a higher-income household. It is a value judgement you choose, not a result the tool dictates; as you change ε, the welfare figure updates to reflect it.

  • ε = 0: every £1 counts equally, regardless of income (pure efficiency; the utilitarian case).
  • ε = 1: the standard central value, a £1 gain to a household at or below the at-risk-of-poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much as the same £1 to a household on the median.
  • ε = 2: strong inequality aversion, the same gain counts about 2.8 times. That is the maximum: the living standard is floored at the at-risk-of-poverty line (AROP), 60% of the median, before the weight is taken.

A bottom-targeted reform, such as a higher minimum income guarantee, grows more valuable as ε rises; a reform whose gains sit higher up the distribution, such as a tax rate cut, shrinks as ε rises.

How to use it

Analyst mode. Set ε, then move one dial or flip the toggle and read the results: the welfare effect, the ε strip (how that effect changes across ε values), the fiscal cost, the winners-and-losers split, and the decile chart. The other controls snap back to baseline whenever you move one.

Provider mode. Enter a caseload and targeting profile, then read the value ladder (defined below). Every value shown includes its source and provenance. The capacity-gap and shock views are indicative only. Their demand elasticities and staff ratios are registry assumptions rather than measured national figures, though the shock anchors, including the share of {{UNITS}} losing an earner, are computed from this country's own shock run.

The value ladder, a stepped set of value estimates, from the most conservative at the bottom to the fullest at the top:

  • Cash floor: the value counting only the direct cash the service moves (benefits paid or income secured). A deliberately conservative lower bound.
  • Headline: the cash floor plus the monetised value of the service's wider social outcomes, for example wellbeing gains. The main figure to quote.
  • Low/central/high band: the range around the headline, reflecting genuine uncertainty in those social-outcome values.

Scenarios mode. {{SCENARIO_COUNT_CAP}} fixed reforms and shocks, each with its fiscal cost, distributional effect, welfare, and cost-effectiveness, plus a ranking that reorders as ε changes and the crossover point where that ranking flips. Unlike the Analyst dials these are fixed points rather than a continuous range, and two of them combine a downturn with a policy response, which the single-reform surface cannot represent.

Methods and reproducibility: uk/docs/METHODS.md (current). Quick start: uk/docs/QUICKSTART.md (current). User guide: Documents/USER_GUIDE_UK_D2_2.pdf (current). Response surface: uk/outputs/dial_grid.json (tracked; the aggregates are embedded in this page).

min_income.base: The Universal Credit standard allowance is the basic monthly UC payment, before extra elements. In 2023-24 it is about £368.74 a month for a single adult aged 25 or over. The dial raises every standard-allowance rate by the shown percentage.
min_income.explain: Raising the basic UC rate lifts the incomes of households on Universal Credit, who sit in the lowest income deciles. It is a pure giveaway to the bottom: there are no losers, and the gain is concentrated in deciles 1 to 3, which is why its welfare value grows as ε (the weight on the poorest) rises.

child_benefit.base: Child Benefit is the weekly payment to families with children. In 2023-24 it is £24.00 a week for the eldest or only child and £15.90 for each other child. The dial raises these rates by the shown percentage.
child_benefit.explain: Raising Child Benefit helps all families with children. Because Child Benefit is not means-tested and families with children sit across the income range, the gain is broader than a UC rise, reaching middle deciles as well as the bottom.

personal_allowance.label: Personal allowance (income tax threshold)
personal_allowance.base: The personal allowance is how much you can earn before paying income tax: £12,570 in 2023-24 (frozen). A higher allowance means less income tax is paid (a tax cut, shown here as a welfare gain); a lower allowance means more tax. The dial moves the allowance by the shown percentage of £12,570, so +20% is about £15,084 and the “raise to £15,000” reform sits at about +19.3%.
personal_allowance.explain: The personal allowance is a broad income-tax cut: it helps almost everyone who pays income tax, so the gain is spread across taxpayers in the middle and upper-middle deciles, with little reaching the very bottom (who pay little or no income tax). A higher allowance is a gain, but its welfare value falls as ε rises because the gains sit higher up.

gdp_shock.base: The microsimulation models the 2023-24 financial year (the 2023 income year), not 2026. A GDP shock of, say, −3% represents the economy contracting 3% from that 2023 base. It is routed through a GDP-to-unemployment relationship, so the loss lands as lost earnings on the households pushed out of work.
gdp_shock.explain: A GDP downturn is modelled as job losses: market (earnings) income falls for the households moved into unemployment. The loss is concentrated in working households that lose earnings, so it reads as a welfare loss with losers but no winners.

unemployment_shock.base: UK unemployment was about 4% in 2023-24. The dial adds the shown percentage points on top (for example +3pp is a rise to about 7%), modelled as that share of currently-employed people losing their earnings.
unemployment_shock.explain: A rise in unemployment removes earnings from the people who lose their jobs, partly cushioned by Universal Credit. The loss is concentrated in the affected working households and deepens as the shock grows.

uc_taper.base: The UC taper is how fast Universal Credit is withdrawn as earnings rise: for every £1 earned above the work allowance, UC falls by the taper rate. The baseline is 55p in the £ (55%). A higher taper (towards 65%) withdraws UC faster, so working claimants keep less; a lower taper (towards 45%) lets them keep more.
uc_taper.explain: The taper affects UC claimants who are in work. Lowering it (towards 45%) lets them keep more UC as they earn, a gain to lower-middle working households; raising it (towards 65%) is a takeaway from the same group. The baseline of 55% is the zero point, with no effect.

uc_work_allowance.base: The work allowance is how much a Universal Credit claimant with children, or with limited capability for work, can earn before the taper starts to reduce their UC. In 2023-24 it is £379 a month if the claimant also receives help with housing costs, or £631 a month if not. The dial raises the work allowance by the shown percentage, so claimants can earn more before any UC is withdrawn.
uc_work_allowance.explain: Raising the work allowance helps working UC claimants with children keep more of their earnings. The gain sits in the lower-middle of the distribution, among working families on UC.

hicbc.base: The High Income Child Benefit Charge claws back Child Benefit from families where someone earns over £50,000 (and all of it above £60,000) in 2023-24. Removing the charge lets these higher-earning families keep their full Child Benefit.
hicbc.explain: Removing the High Income Child Benefit Charge restores Child Benefit to higher-earning families, so the gain sits higher up the income distribution. That is why its welfare value falls as ε (the weight on the poorest) rises.

profiles_provenance_note: Targeting bands defined as decile groups (1 to 3, 4 to 6, and all ten). A presentational choice about which part of the distribution a service serves, with no source; the user selects among them.

labels.cb_remove_hicbc: Remove High Income Child Benefit Charge

data.crossover: ε = 1.62 — gdp_minus_3_plus_uc_boost overtakes raise_personal_allowance (dense [1.5,2.0] grid, root 1.621)

provenance_note.du3: The modelled shock magnitude, 3pp, a computed point on this country's surface.
provenance_note.du5: The modelled shock magnitude, 5pp, a computed point on this country's surface.
provenance_note.aff3: Working-age units whose employment income falls at the modelled 3pp shock, computed from this country's own shock run: 466,700 units, 2.98 per cent of the 15,641,500 working-age units that hold employment income. Units in which every adult is 65 or over are excluded, which removes 5,200 units the shock also touched. The shock zeroes one earner per selected unit, so this is equally the count of people who lose their main job. It is not a count of everyone in an affected unit, which would be about 2.4 times larger.
provenance_note.aff5: Working-age units whose employment income falls at the modelled 5pp shock, computed from this country's own shock run: 782,500 units, 5.00 per cent of the 15,641,500 working-age units that hold employment income. Units in which every adult is 65 or over are excluded, which removes 6,600 units the shock also touched. The shock zeroes one earner per selected unit, so this is equally the count of people who lose their main job. It is not a count of everyone in an affected unit, which would be about 2.4 times larger.
provenance_note.dpov3: Change in relative poverty after housing costs at 3pp, from this country's own scenario aggregates: 28.428 per cent at baseline to 29.083 per cent at shock_3pp, a rise of 0.654pp.
provenance_note.dpov5: Change in relative poverty after housing costs at 5pp, from this country's own scenario aggregates: 28.428 per cent at baseline to 29.429 per cent at shock_5pp, a rise of 1.001pp.

provenance_note.staffRatio: Registry staff_ratio = 120, in a unit the registry does not state. Remains an assumption. The service attribution, 'DWP; direct proportional relationship with unemployment', covers the demand relationship and the caseload, not the staffing. UNIT UNESTABLISHED. The registry states no unit for this field: every service_demand entry carries unit 'service params' and nothing per field, its `range` covers only demand_elasticity, and not one of the ten source strings mentions staff, caseworkers or caseloads. The values read as concurrent caseloads (15 for children's social care, 25 for domestic abuse, 120 for a work coach) rather than the annual throughput that a gap measured in cases per year would need, but nothing on file establishes either reading, so the value is left exactly as it is. No formula in the tool reads this parameter: the extra-caseworker figure is computed from the provider's own stated cases per caseworker per year. It is carried here as a documented benchmark, not as an input.
provenance_note.unitCost: No cost attribution and no price year. The service attribution, 'DWP; direct proportional relationship with unemployment', covers the demand relationship, not the cost per case. PRICE BASE: this value is an ASSUMPTION STATED AT THE 2024-equivalent base, not a figure uprated from a source year. It carries no independent vintage to preserve, so declaring it at the panel base is the only coherent option; it is not evidence that a 2024-25 source was consulted.

provenance_note.unitCost: GBP 4488 at 2024-25 prices. Source: National Audit Office, Tackling problem drug use, HC 297, session 2009-10, at 2008-09 prices, GBP 3,000, the attribution carried in the technical report and the provenance registry and preferred over the bibliography's NDTMS claim. SCOPE, AN EXTRAPOLATION: nothing in the source covers alcohol. Figure 5 is drug treatment budgets, the corroborating paragraph refers to adult drug treatment, and the agency's remit as the report states it is treatment for drug dependency in England. This row is labelled drug and alcohol treatment, so applying the figure to a combined population extends it beyond the population it was measured on, and no alcohol-treatment source has been substituted for it. DENOMINATOR: effective treatment is defined at the report's note 2, in three parts, and covers adults discharged twelve weeks or more after triage, adults still in treatment at twelve weeks, and adults discharged within twelve weeks in a planned way. The third limb admits people treated for less than twelve weeks, so the shorthand 'twelve weeks or more' overstates the treatment intensity the denominator represents. ROUNDING: GBP 3,000 is the source's own rounding of GBP 2,979, so this figure inherits about 0.7 per cent of upward rounding from the source. ALTERNATIVE NOT TAKEN: the same report gives a genuinely costed unit price of GBP 4,900 at paragraph 18, from a treatment outcomes study. That is a different concept sitting GBP 1,900 away in the same document, and the budget-based figure has been taken deliberately in preference to it. Uprated on the HM Treasury GDP deflator, ONS series L8GG, financial-year index, March 2026 vintage: 2008-09 = 66.8397, 2024-25 = 100.0, factor 1.496117. PRICE BASE: 2024-equivalent (2024-25), the provider tab's own base, uprated to it from the source's 2008-09; the target base was confirmed from PROVIDER_TOOLREADY_2024 rather than assumed.

Jobcentre Plus / DWP work coaches.provenance_note: Non-pecuniary wellbeing of moving into employment. CHAIN: 0.46 WELLBY (Clark, Fleche, Layard, Powdthavee and Ward 2018, Table 4.2, a Britain fixed-effects estimate) x GBP 16,300, the applied spine, = GBP 7,498.00 raw; x 0.30, an effect share; x 0.22, attribution; = GBP 494.868. ORIGIN 16300 FACTOR 0.46; BAND ORIGIN 12540 AND 20064; BAND FACTOR 0.30 AND 0.55; STAGE EFFECT 0.11 0.30 0.46 ATTRIBUTION 0.20 0.22 0.27. THE STAGE RULE: an outcome value is raw x effect share x attribution. Where the effect share is ALREADY AN IMPACT net of a comparison group the attribution is 1.0, because the counterfactual is inside the number and deducting it a second time understates the value; where the effect share is an OBSERVED OUTCOME RATE the attribution is what removes the counterfactual. EFFECT SHARE, an OUTCOME RATE. CENTRAL 0.30: the Work and Health Programme job-outcome rate of 31 per cent and the Restart Scheme job-outcome rate of 30 per cent, which converge; taken at 0.30. LOW 0.11: Additional Work Coach Support, 11 per cent of participants in work at twelve months. HIGH 0.46: the Work and Health Programme first-earnings rate of 46 per cent. DENOMINATORS, confirmed at the publications: the Work and Health Programme rates are per PROGRAMME START, not per referral, measured within 24 months, over 350,000 starts from 510,000 referrals between November 2017 and February 2024 with a full 24-month opportunity, a referral-to-start conversion of 68 per cent (DWP, Work and Health Programme Official Statistics to February 2026); first earnings exclude self-employment. The Restart rate is per start with at least twelve months of support, 840,000 starts between July 2021 and April 2025, a job outcome being cumulative earnings equivalent to 16 hours a week for 26 weeks at the National Living Wage (DWP, Restart Scheme statistics to April 2026); its first-earnings rate is 44 per cent. The Additional Work Coach Support rate is per participant, new and existing Universal Credit and Employment and Support Allowance customers with a health condition or disability, at twelve months. ATTRIBUTION, an IMPACT net of a comparison group, sourced at both ends. LOW 0.20: the Department's own Restart business case projects sustained jobs for an additional six in a hundred participants above what would have happened without the scheme, and six over the thirty in a hundred who reach a job outcome is 0.20. THE SIX IN A HUNDRED IS THE DEPARTMENT'S OWN BUSINESS-CASE PROJECTION AND NOT A STATISTICAL FINDING. It is published in House of Commons Committee of Public Accounts, The Restart Scheme for Long-term Unemployed People, Forty-Second Report of Session 2022-23, HC 733, 22 March 2023, at Conclusions and recommendations paragraph 1, where the committee quotes the Department's expectation of a return of 2.44 pounds for every pound spent and its estimate that an extra six in a hundred participants will find sustained work above what would have happened anyway, and warns in the same sentence that if that estimate is too high the benefits of the scheme will quickly fall away. The committee measured nothing here; it is reporting what the Department expected. HIGH 0.27: Additional Work Coach Support reached 11 per cent in work against 8 per cent in a matched comparison at twelve months, an impact of three percentage points, and three over eleven is 0.2727. THE PUBLICATION IS Department for Work and Pensions, The impact of additional Jobcentre Plus support on the employment outcomes of disabled people, research and analysis, 18 March 2025, which states that twelve months after the intervention 11 per cent of participants were in work compared to 8 per cent of the comparison group, a 3 percentage point employment impact, and that the impact is statistically significant. It is NOT the qualitative report The experience of Additional Work Coach Support of 2 May 2025, which carries no percentage at all and refers the reader to this impact analysis. A LATER PUBLICATION RESTATES THE SAME TWELVE-MONTH COMPARISON AND THIS VALUE DOES NOT FOLLOW IT: the extended impact assessment at 24 months, Official Statistics, 25 March 2026, gives 11 per cent against 8.2 per cent, an impact of 2.8 percentage points, which on the same arithmetic would put this bound at 2.8 over 11 = 0.2545 rather than 0.2727. The shipped 0.27 is the March 2025 figure and is unchanged; the restatement is recorded here so the difference is accounted for rather than left for a reader to find. The effect share's low bound of 0.11 is unaffected, because both publications put the participant rate at 11 per cent. THE CENTRAL OF 0.22 IS A CHOICE WITHIN THAT SOURCED RANGE AND IS NOT ITSELF A COMPUTED QUANTITY: it sits nearer the Restart end because Restart is the larger programme and the one whose figure is the Department's own additionality estimate rather than an evaluation of a different intervention. Nothing derives 0.22 exactly, and this note says so rather than implying otherwise. Computed from UK sources. PRICE BASE: 2024-equivalent (2024-25), the provider tab's own base.

UC claim processing (DWP).provenance_note: The processing and averted-hardship limb is UNEVIDENCED-EXCLUDED and valued at zero; no effect size was found. The zero is the modelling decision, not a measurement. THE STAGE RULE: an outcome value is raw x effect share x attribution. Where the effect share is ALREADY AN IMPACT net of a comparison group the attribution is 1.0, because the counterfactual is inside the number and deducting it a second time understates the value; where the effect share is an OBSERVED OUTCOME RATE the attribution is what removes the counterfactual. Every point in this row is zero, and zero multiplied by any pair of stages is zero. Under the rule the entitlement limb is an ENGINE route and is excluded from the outcomes sum in any case, and the hardship limb has no effect size of either kind, so there is no quantity for an attribution to act on. PRICE BASE: 2024-equivalent (2024-25), the provider tab's own base.

Debt advice (Citizens Advice, StepChange.provenance_note: Improved mental health from debt advice. CHAIN: the central is GBP 0 by decision and not by omission, from Pleasence and Balmer 2007, a UK randomised trial with a null result; the low is GBP 0 for the same reason. The high is 0.5 WELLBY x GBP 20,064, the high spine tier, = GBP 10,032 raw; x 0.63, an effect share; x 0.5, attribution; = GBP 3,160.08. ORIGIN 16300 FACTOR 0.4; BAND ORIGIN 12540 AND 20064; BAND FACTOR 0.3 AND 0.5; STAGE EFFECT 0 0 0.63 ATTRIBUTION 1.0 1.0 0.5. THE STAGE RULE: an outcome value is raw x effect share x attribution. Where the effect share is ALREADY AN IMPACT net of a comparison group the attribution is 1.0, because the counterfactual is inside the number and deducting it a second time understates the value; where the effect share is an OBSERVED OUTCOME RATE the attribution is what removes the counterfactual. THIS ROW MIXES THE TWO CASES AND IS THE CLEAREST ILLUSTRATION OF THE RULE. The central rests on a null randomised result, which is an impact net of a comparison group, so its attribution is 1.0; a null multiplied by anything is still a null, so the attribution changes no value here. The high rests on the MaPS 2023/24 self-report in which 52 to 63 per cent of clients report improvement, which is an OUTCOME RATE, and a self-reported one, on a denominator of clients advised rather than of people in problem debt; it therefore takes an attribution, and it takes the documented default of 0.5 because no study of debt advice supplies an attributable fraction. That 0.5 is the tool's own SROI-style modelling assumption, recorded in uk/docs/TECHNICAL_REPORT.md section 7 and PROVIDER_DECISIONS.md item 9, and is not taken from any published default. Because the central is zero, the shipped value-added of this service is zero at every catchment and only the high end moves. UK sources. PRICE BASE: 2024-equivalent (2024-25), the provider tab's own base.

NHS Talking Therapies (IAPT).provenance_note: Recovery from depression or anxiety. CHAIN: 0.71 WELLBY central (Clark et al. 2018) x GBP 16,300 = GBP 11,573.00 raw; x 0.5, an effect share; x 0.6, attribution; = GBP 3,471.90. ORIGIN 16300 FACTOR 0.71; BAND ORIGIN 12540 AND 20064; BAND FACTOR 0.71 AND 1.5; STAGE EFFECT 0.4 0.5 0.6 ATTRIBUTION 0.455 0.60 0.610. THE STAGE RULE: an outcome value is raw x effect share x attribution. Where the effect share is ALREADY AN IMPACT net of a comparison group the attribution is 1.0, because the counterfactual is inside the number and deducting it a second time understates the value; where the effect share is an OBSERVED OUTCOME RATE the attribution is what removes the counterfactual. EFFECT SHARE 0.50, an OUTCOME RATE, SOURCED and unchanged: NHS England Digital, NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety and depression, Annual reports and Monthly statistics; 50.9 per cent at March 2024, 50.5 per cent in the 2024-25 annual report, 0.5005 for July 2025, four further months in a 49.7 to 51.6 per cent range. DENOMINATOR: referrals at caseness WHO FINISH A COURSE of treatment, the publication's own recovery denominator, not all referrals; about 37 per cent of referrals finish a course, so this share must not be applied to an undifferentiated referral caseload. It does not reproduce reliable improvement, which runs 67 to 68 per cent. ATTRIBUTION 0.60, an IMPACT net of a comparison group, sits inside the sourced range its band comes from. LOW 0.455: the Norwegian Prompt Mental Health Care trial, DOI 10.1159/000504453, the closest institutional analogue to a national talking-therapies service. HIGH 0.610: Cuijpers et al. 2021, DOI 10.1111/acps.13335, the attributable fraction against waitlist across 228 randomised trials. The same synthesis gives 0.585 against care as usual, which is the more conservative comparison and is recorded here because it is the one an appraiser should reach for when the counterfactual is an existing service rather than nothing. An unsourced 0.4 to 0.8 band is not used. This central and its band depart from the documented 0.5 default and its 0.3 to 0.7 band, and the departure is evidenced. The sensitivity row beside this one, GBP 7,500 on a QALY valuation, is shown for comparison and is not added to the headline. Computed from UK sources. PRICE BASE: 2024-equivalent (2024-25), the provider tab's own base.

Housing / homelessness services.provenance_note: Averted homelessness and rough sleeping. CHAIN: GBP 20,128 per person per year of averted public-sector cost (Crisis 2015, Pleace; DCLG), a 12-month rough-sleeper vignette and a derived estimate rather than a surveyed average; x 1.3406, uprating to 2024-25; x 0.2, an effect share; x 0.562, attribution; = GBP 3,032.95628. ORIGIN 20128 FACTOR 1.3406; BAND ORIGIN 15000 AND 35000; STAGE EFFECT 0.1 0.2 0.35 ATTRIBUTION 0.500 0.562 0.575. THE STAGE RULE: an outcome value is raw x effect share x attribution. Where the effect share is ALREADY AN IMPACT net of a comparison group the attribution is 1.0, because the counterfactual is inside the number and deducting it a second time understates the value; where the effect share is an OBSERVED OUTCOME RATE the attribution is what removes the counterfactual. EFFECT SHARE 0.20: NOT SOURCED, AND DECLARED AN ASSUMPTION. QUANTITY: intended as an outcome rate. The reason it stays and the reason it cannot be sourced are the same. Every published rate in this field is post-placement tenancy sustainment, 80 to 96 per cent, and its denominator is PEOPLE ALREADY HOUSED, so it does not measure what this multiplier is applied to, which is a whole referred caseload. Converting one to the other needs a referral-to-placement conversion rate, and nobody publishes one. A comparator the project already holds and does not use is the Hogar Si and Provivienda Habitat evaluation, 96.06 per cent retention at 18 months on an experimental design, which is on the same already-housed denominator and so does not close the gap either. The 0.20 is therefore carried as an assumption with its reason, not as a rate with a source. ATTRIBUTION, an IMPACT net of a comparison group, SOURCED. The three fractions all come from the Canadian At Home / Chez Soi randomised trial. LOW 0.500: at two years, 62 per cent of Housing First participants were housed all of the time against 31 per cent of treatment as usual, and 31 over 62 is 0.500 (Mental Health Commission of Canada, national cross-site final report). CENTRAL 0.562: over the trial, Housing First participants spent 73 per cent of their time stably housed against 32 per cent, and 41 over 73 is 0.5616. HIGH 0.575: at one year, 73 per cent of Housing First participants and 31 per cent of treatment as usual resided in stable housing, and 42 over 73 is 0.5753 (Aubry, Tsemberis, Adair and colleagues, One-Year Outcomes of a Randomized Controlled Trial of Housing First With ACT in Five Canadian Cities, Psychiatric Services 2015, 66(5), 463 to 469, DOI 10.1176/appi.ps.201400167; n = 950, 469 Housing First and 481 treatment as usual). The central is the median of the three and is the time-in-stable-housing measure, which is the one closest in kind to an annual averted cost. A SCOPE MISMATCH THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THESE THREE FRACTIONS: the trials are an INTENSIVE HOUSING FIRST MODEL with assertive community treatment, for people with severe mental illness who were absolutely homeless or precariously housed, in five Canadian cities. THIS ROW IS GENERIC HOUSING SUPPORT. The attribution is borrowed from a stronger intervention on a more disadvantaged population than the row describes, which is more likely to overstate the fraction than to understate it. UK source for the cost, Canadian for the attribution. PRICE BASE: 2024-equivalent (2024-25), the provider tab's own base.

Children's social care.provenance_note: Averted entry to care. CHAIN: GBP 89,390 discounted lifetime cost per averted case (Conti, Morris, Melnychuk and Pizzo for the NSPCC) x 1.2979, uprating to 2024-25, = GBP 116,018.08; x 0.086, the 8.6 percentage-point family group conferencing effect; x 1.0, attribution; = GBP 9,977.658166. ORIGIN 89390 FACTOR 1.2979; BAND ORIGIN 89390 AND 145508; STAGE EFFECT 0 0.086 0.086 ATTRIBUTION 1.0 1.0 1.0. THE STAGE RULE: an outcome value is raw x effect share x attribution. Where the effect share is ALREADY AN IMPACT net of a comparison group the attribution is 1.0, because the counterfactual is inside the number and deducting it a second time understates the value; where the effect share is an OBSERVED OUTCOME RATE the attribution is what removes the counterfactual. WHY THE ATTRIBUTION IS 1.0. The 8.6 percentage points are the DIFFERENCE BETWEEN TWO ARMS of the Foundations and Coram family group conferencing randomised controlled trial, 44.8 per cent care entry in the control arm against 36.2 per cent in the treated arm. That is an IMPACT, not an outcome rate: the counterfactual is already deducted by the trial's own design. An attribution of 0.5 here would deduct it a second time and halve the value. THE BAND COMES FROM THE SOURCE RATHER THAN FROM THE MULTIPLIERS. Conti and colleagues publish a 95 per cent interval of GBP 44,896 to GBP 145,508 around that central, and the high is the upper bound of that interval. THE LOW IS THE NULL, AND WHY. Two lows are available. (a) The Nurmatov et al. 2020 systematic review finds no overall reduction in care entry, an effect of zero, which gives GBP 0. (b) The lower bound of the Conti interval, GBP 44,896 at the central effect, gives GBP 5,011.264582. THE NULL IS APPLIED. It is the stronger claim about the low end: a cost-interval low still presumes the effect is real and only asks how much a case costs, whereas the null asks whether there is an effect at all, and a published review saying there is not is the more informative floor. The Conti lower bound is recorded here so that a reader who prefers it can see what it would give. UK sources. PRICE BASE: 2024-equivalent (2024-25), the provider tab's own base.

Domestic abuse services.provenance_note: Averted or reduced domestic abuse. CHAIN: GBP 34,015 per victim (Home Office RR107, Oliver, Alexander, Roe and Wlasny 2019, at 2016/17 prices and itself derived as about GBP 66bn over about 1,946,000 victims rather than measured per victim); x 1.3143, uprating to 2024-25, = GBP 44,705.9145; x 0.24, an effect share; x 13/24, attribution; = GBP 5,811.768885. ORIGIN 34015 FACTOR 1.3143; BAND ORIGIN 20000 AND 73560; STAGE EFFECT 0.24 0.24 0.24 ATTRIBUTION 0.5416667 0.5416667 0.5416667. THE STAGE RULE: an outcome value is raw x effect share x attribution. Where the effect share is ALREADY AN IMPACT net of a comparison group the attribution is 1.0, because the counterfactual is inside the number and deducting it a second time understates the value; where the effect share is an OBSERVED OUTCOME RATE the attribution is what removes the counterfactual. WHY THE COCHRANE ODDS RATIO IS NOT THE SOURCE. An effect share of 0.25 CANNOT BE PRODUCED FROM THAT ODDS RATIO AT ANY BASELINE: the largest absolute reduction in the probability of abuse an odds ratio can give is (1 - sqrt(OR)) / (1 + sqrt(OR)), which is 0.2079 at OR 0.43 and 0.2311 at OR 0.39, both below 0.25. An odds ratio is also the wrong kind of quantity for this slot, being an impact net of a comparison group, so pairing it with an attribution would deduct the counterfactual twice. BUILT ON THE TRIAL'S OWN ARMS. Sullivan and Bybee 1999, Reducing violence using community-based advocacy for women with abusive partners, Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 67(1), 43 to 53, DOI 10.1037/0022-006x.67.1.43, report that 24 PER CENT OF WOMEN WHO WORKED WITH ADVOCATES EXPERIENCED NO PHYSICAL ABUSE across the two years of post-intervention follow-up, by the original assailant or by any new partner, AGAINST 11 PER CENT OF CONTROLS. EFFECT SHARE 0.24, the treated-arm OUTCOME RATE. ATTRIBUTION 13 over 24, which is 0.541667 recurring, the share of that outcome not also observed in the control arm. The arithmetic: 24 minus 11 is 13; 13 over 24 is 0.5416667; and 0.24 x 13/24 is 0.13 EXACTLY, so the combined multiplier is a clean 0.13 and the two stages multiply to a figure a reader can check in their head. WHAT THE ESTIMATE ATTACHES TO, and it is narrower than this row: intensive advocacy of TWELVE HOURS OR MORE, women recruited ON EXIT FROM REFUGES, principally UNITED STATES trials, significant at 24 months and not significant at 12 or 36 months, on evidence the review rates low to very low. This row is generic domestic abuse service provision, so the effect is borrowed from a more intensive intervention and a narrower population than the row describes. THE BAND COMES ONLY FROM THE COST PER VICTIM, GBP 20,000 to GBP 73,560, a factor of 3.7. A single trial's arm rates carry no published interval, so the multipliers contribute no width. The sensitivity row beside this one, GBP 2,608 on a felt-safety wellbeing valuation, is shown for comparison and is not added to the headline. UK source for the cost, United States trial for both multipliers. PRICE BASE: 2024-equivalent (2024-25), the provider tab's own base.

Drug & alcohol treatment.provenance_note: Chain: GBP 3,000 per adult in effective treatment (National Audit Office, Tackling problem drug use, HC 297 session 2009-10, Figure 5, at 2008-09 prices); x 1.4959, uprating to 2024-25; x 2.5, a benefit-cost ratio; x 1.0, attribution; = GBP 11,219.25, the central figure shipped. ORIGIN 3000 FACTOR 1.4959; BAND ORIGIN 3000 AND 3000; STAGE EFFECT 2.3 2.5 4.0 ATTRIBUTION 1.0 1.0 1.0. Under the stage rule the effect-share slot holds a benefit-cost ratio measured against a constructed no-treatment comparison group, so the counterfactual is inside it and the attribution is 1.0. All three points reproduce exactly from the DATA_OUTCOMES sheet of uk/tools/_superseded/valuation_tool.xlsx, row 20, which carries the ratio at 2.3 / 2.5 / 4.0 and the attribution at 1.0 / 1.0 / 1.0: low GBP 10,321.71 = 3,000 x 1.4959 x 2.3; high GBP 17,950.80 = 3,000 x 1.4959 x 4.0. UPRATING FACTOR 1.4959: the HM Treasury GDP deflator factor from 2008-09 to 2024-25, ONS series L8GG, financial-year index, 2024-25 = 100, December 2025 Quarterly National Accounts vintage published 6 January 2026, on which the 2008-09 index is 66.8478 and 100 / 66.8478 = 1.495936. The unit-cost layer carries the same cost at the March 2026 vintage factor of 1.496117, so this row and services[Drug and alcohol treatment].unitCost sit on different vintages of the same series. THE BAND ENDS: 2.3 is the Black review 2021, Annex C Table C1, year one; 4.0 is Public Health England 2018. ATTRIBUTION 1.00: DEFENSIBLE AS AN APPRAISAL CONVENTION, NOT AS AN EMPIRICAL RATE. QUANTITY: neither an outcome rate nor an impact; it is the deliberate absence of a second counterfactual step. The reasoning is that a benefit-cost ratio built on benefits incremental to business as usual has already made the counterfactual adjustment, so applying an attribution on top would count it twice. THE CONDITION HAS BEEN CHECKED AND HOLDS. The central 2.5 is the Drug Treatment Outcomes Research Study cost-effectiveness analysis (Davies, Jones, Vamvakas, Dubourg and Donmall, Home Office Research Report 25, 2nd edition, December 2009, ISBN 978 1 84987 124 2), whose benefits are measured against a constructed no-treatment comparison group, not gross: net treatment cost GBP 4,531, offset by GBP 6,450 of savings in health, social care and offending, plus a QALY gain valued at GBP 30,000 per QALY, giving a net benefit of GBP 6,527 and a ratio of about 2.5 to 1. SO 1.0 IS SUPPORTED, with one qualification the source states itself: the study had no control group, and the comparison set was built by assuming that the costs and quality-adjusted life years observed at the baseline interview would have stayed constant over the follow-up year, so the report calls its results suggestive of possible benefits rather than indicative of causation. The counterfactual adjustment has therefore been made once, by assumption rather than by an experimental contrast. DENOMINATOR of the ratio: all participants who had a triage assessment and a care plan for structured Tier 3 or Tier 4 treatment, whether or not they started or completed it, over one year of scheduled follow-up, and it excludes the costs of referral schemes such as the Drug Interventions Programme. NOTE ALSO that the effect-share slot in this row holds a benefit-cost ratio rather than a share, which is why its value exceeds one. UK sources. PRICE BASE: 2024-equivalent (2024-25), the provider tab's own base.

Additional GP consultations.provenance_note: COST-INPUT: valued at the cost of provision with no separate outcome, so the outcome value is zero by decision. The underlying consultation price is PSSRU-sourced; the zero value-added is the modelling choice.

data.bu_provenance_note: The count this block reports as its national scale: working-age benefit units in millions for the UK (21.443496, matching the surface's own units_k of 21,443.494) and working-age POPULATION in millions for the three EU blocks. Because it means two different things it is not used for any per-unit arithmetic: the per-unit welfare figure and the affected fraction both read units_k from the surface instead. Retained as the documented national scale and as a fallback if a surface ever arrives without a population_basis.

population_basis.includes: Benefit units with at least one adult aged 18 to 64.
population_basis.excludes: Units in which every adult is 65 or over.
population_basis.summary: Working-age units only, meaning benefit units with at least one adult aged 18 to 64, excluding units in which every adult is 65 or over.

meta.note: Single-reform magnitude grids; one lever per point; the baseline is the zero point of each dial; HICBC removal is a binary toggle. WEVM and decile contributions are in GBP millions, median-anchored and AROP-floored, equivalised.

units.fiscal: GBP millions versus baseline; net_exchequer_cost_m = benefit_delta_m - income_tax_delta_m - sic_delta_m - ni_employer_delta_m, positive is a cost to the exchequer. sic_delta_m is the employee contribution and ni_employer_delta_m the employer one; both enter the identity.
units.poverty: levels, not deltas: headcounts of people in thousands, poverty gaps in GBP millions, anchored_bhc_threshold_cur in GBP of equivalised annual income, with population_k and units_k as the denominators a rate needs
units.winlose: the weighted count of benefit units with a gain, and with a loss, each over the weighted count of all benefit units, times 100. Shares of benefit units, not of people, unlike every poverty headcount in the same object, which counts people. Both rows are labelled with this base on the tool face.

meta.poverty_basis: Two thresholds, both emitted at every point. RELATIVE (relative_*): PolicyEngine's own relative low-income line, which moves with the median, so a reform that lowers incomes generally lowers the line and can cut the measured count without anyone being better off. ANCHORED (anchored_*): 60% of the weighted median equivalised (OECD-modified) household income computed once at the zero-magnitude baseline point and held fixed across every point of every dial, emitted as anchored_bhc_threshold_cur so it is auditable; the right comparison of a reform against its own baseline. The anchored line is this project's own AROP construction, identical to the EU builder's, so the anchored series is the same measure in all four countries; it is NOT PolicyEngine's line, so the anchored and relative counts do not coincide at the baseline. ANCHORED IS NOT ABSOLUTE: absolute_* is PolicyEngine's fixed-base-year measure and is unchanged.
